* Cyclique is a **desktop app for organisers of recreational cycling groups in Singapore**, optimised for use through a Command Line Interface (CLI) while still giving you the benefits of a Graphical User Interface (GUI).

* Organisers often have their riders' contact and information scattered across chats, spreadsheets, and memory, making it hard to tell who's actually suitable for a given ride. Cyclique keeps this information in one place and helps you quickly find which riders suit a ride, based on experience, location, availability, and preferences.

* It's built for organisers who need to manage a significant number of cyclists, quickly access cyclists' contact and emergency information, and identify available cyclists by factors such as preferred cycling location, FTP, and experience level.

This project uses Gradle for **build automation and dependency management**. **We recommend reading [this Gradle tutorial from se-edu/guides](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/gradle.html).**
The following commands perform common Gradle tasks.
* **`clean`**: Deletes the files created during the previous build tasks (e.g. files in the `build` folder).
* **`shadowJar`**: Uses the Shadow plugin to create the fat JAR file `build/libs/cyclique.jar`.
**`runShadow`**: Builds the application as a fat JAR, then runs it.
* **`checkstyleMain`**: Runs the code style check for the main code base.
**`checkstyleTest`**: Runs the code style check for the test code base.
* `./gradlew clean test`: Cleans the project before running all tests
This project uses GitHub Actions for CI. The necessary workflow configuration files are in `.github/workflows`. No further setup is required.
As part of CI, Gradle generates JaCoCo coverage reports from the tests, and CI uploads the coverage data to Codecov. Codecov then provides information about test coverage.

However, because Codecov is known to run into intermittent problems (e.g., report upload fails) due to issues on the Codecov service side, the CI is configured to pass even if the Codecov task failed. Therefore, developers are advised to check the code coverage levels periodically and take corrective actions if the coverage level falls below desired levels.
To enable Codecov for forks of this project, follow the steps given in [this se-edu guide](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/codecov.html).

The following provides a quick overview of the main components and their interactions.

**`Main`** (consisting of classes [`Main`](https://github.com/se-edu/addressbook-level3/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/Main.java) and [`MainApp`](https://github.com/se-edu/addressbook-level3/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/MainApp.java)) is in charge of the app launch and shut down.
* At app launch, it initializes the other components in the correct sequence, and connects them up with each other.
* At shut down, it shuts down the other components and invokes cleanup methods where necessary.
The bulk of the app's work is done by the following four components:
* [**`Model`**](#model-component): Holds the data of the App in memory.
* [**`Storage`**](#storage-component): Reads data from, and writes data to, the hard disk.
[**`Commons`**](#common-classes) represents a collection of classes used by multiple other components.

This section describes some noteworthy details on how certain features are implemented.
`LogicManager` resolves `delete PHONE` against the displayed list using
missing/hidden-target and ambiguous-target errors before a prompt is shown.
It stores the pending command and an immutable snapshot of that cyclist in memory,
then returns a confirmation request to the existing result panel without executing
or saving the deletion. The command box accepts the next reply through the same
Replies are trimmed and compared ignoring case. `y`/`yes` executes the pending
`DeleteCommand` and saves the book; `n`/`no` clears the request without changing the
model, filter or file. Before execution, the target must still be displayed and
have the same details as the snapshot. Confirmation state is consumed before
execution, so errors or failed saves cannot replay the deletion. Storage failures
retain the existing behaviour and error messages.
An unrecognised reply reports an error and retains the request. A supported command
word, including one with invalid arguments, cancels the request before normal
parsing/execution. Cancellation feedback is prepended to the new output or error;
Help and Exit flags are preserved. `AddressBookParser.isRecognisedCommand` makes
this distinction using the same case-sensitive command words. Another delete
replaces the pending request after validating its own phone target. Pending requests
are never serialised and disappear when the application closes or restarts.

`Person` stores an `Optional<Phone>` emergency contact as a data field. New `add` commands require `sos/`; `edit` optionally replaces it and otherwise preserves it. All supplied numbers reuse `ParserUtil.parsePhone`, including repeated `sos/` find criteria. Find uses OR within each field and AND across supplied fields. Emergency contacts do not participate in cyclist identity because riders may share a contact. Edit and delete still target the cyclist’s own phone number.

`JsonAdaptedPerson` saves the `emergencyPhone` property. Missing or null values load as `Optional.empty()` for backwards compatibility, while supplied invalid values reject the record. `PersonCard` shows the number in a labelled SOS row, or **Not provided** for legacy records. Help formats and dropdown templates include the new prefix.
`rideadd n/NAME from/FROM to/TO l/LOCATION d/DISTANCE f/MINIMUM_POWER s/MAX_GROUP_SIZE [notes/NOTES]`
creates a group ride. The diagrams are not updated for rides yet and are deferred to a later increment.
**Model.** A `Ride` (package `seedu.address.model.ride`) is immutable and holds an `int` ID, a `Name`, two
`RideDateTime` values (`from` and `to`), a `Location`, a `Distance`, a `MinimumPower`, a `GroupSize`, an
`Optional<Notes>` and a roster. `Name` and `Location` are reused from the cyclist model, so a ride follows the
same name and location rules as a cyclist. Every other field is a small value class with its own
`isValidXyz` method and `MESSAGE_CONSTRAINTS`, in the same style as `Ftp` and `Phone`:
* `RideDateTime` accepts only `DD-MM-YYYY TTTT`. A regular expression fixes the digit counts, and a strict
`java.time` formatter then rejects dates that do not exist (such as 31 February) and times outside 0000 to 2359.
* `Distance` is a positive number of kilometres with up to 2 decimal places, stored in its simplest form so that
* `MinimumPower` is a whole number from 1 to 600 watts, the same range as `Ftp`. It is a separate class so that its
error message talks about minimum power instead of FTP.
* `GroupSize` is a positive whole number. `Notes` has at most 10 words, and repeated spaces are collapsed.
* The roster is an unmodifiable list of cyclist phone numbers. A new ride starts with an empty roster. Phone
numbers are used because a cyclist's phone number is already how cyclists are identified.
`Ride`'s constructor rejects a `to` that is earlier than `from`, using `Ride.isValidPeriod`. A ride that ends at
the moment it starts is allowed.
**ID assignment.** The parser builds a ride whose ID is `Ride.UNASSIGNED_ID` (0). `Model#addRide` passes it to
`AddressBook#addRide`, which gives it the current `nextRideId`, increments the counter and returns the stored ride.
The ID is therefore decided in one place and `RideAddCommand` shows the stored ride to the user. IDs are never
reused, because the counter only goes up and is saved with the data. `AddressBook#setRides` raises the counter if it
is lower than the highest ride ID, so a hand-edited file cannot cause a clash. Rides are told apart by ID, so two
rides with identical details are allowed and `rideadd` has no duplicate check.
`notes/`. Prefixes are only recognised after whitespace, so `notes/` is not confused with `n/` and `to/` is not
confused with a word that happens to end in `to`. Rides reuse `PREFIX_NAME`, `PREFIX_LOCATION` and `PREFIX_FTP`
`PREFIX_NOTES`. A missing compulsory field or a non-empty preamble gives the usual invalid-format message with
`RideAddCommand.MESSAGE_USAGE`, a repeated prefix is reported by `verifyNoDuplicatePrefixesFor`, and each field is
parsed by a `ParserUtil` method that throws the field's own message. Values are checked in the order name, `from`,
`to`, location, distance, minimum power, group size and notes, and only the first error is reported. The check
that `to/` is not earlier than `from/` runs after every field is valid.
**Storage.** Rides are saved in the same `data/addressbook.json`, in a `rides` array, with a `nextRideId` number.
`JsonAdaptedRide` mirrors `Ride` and validates each field when loading, throwing an `IllegalValueException` with the
field's message. `rides` and `nextRideId` are optional when reading, so files saved before rides existed load with
no rides and `nextRideId` 1. Duplicate ride IDs or a non-positive `nextRideId` make the file invalid. If
`nextRideId` is missing, numbering continues after the highest saved ID.
* *Where the ID is assigned.* Assigning it in the model keeps the parser free of state and keeps all numbering in
one class. The alternative, a counter inside the parser, would be lost on restart and would be hard to test.
* *Where rides are stored.* Keeping rides in `AddressBook` means they are saved by the existing storage code after
every command. A separate rides file would need its own load and save path and could get out of step with the
* *Dates.* `java.time.LocalDateTime` is used, with a strict parser, so invalid dates are rejected by the library
instead of by hand-written checks. Time zones are not needed because every ride is local to the organiser.

The proposed undo/redo mechanism is facilitated by `VersionedAddressBook`. It extends `AddressBook` with an undo/redo history, stored internally as an `addressBookStateList` and `currentStatePointer`. Additionally, it implements the following operations:
* `VersionedAddressBook#commit()` — Saves the current address book state in its history.
* `VersionedAddressBook#undo()` — Restores the previous address book state from its history.
* `VersionedAddressBook#redo()` — Restores a previously undone address book state from its history.
These operations are exposed in the `Model` interface as `Model#commitAddressBook()`, `Model#undoAddressBook()` and `Model#redoAddressBook()` respectively.
Given below is an example usage scenario and how the undo/redo mechanism behaves at each step.

Step 1. The user launches the application for the first time. The `VersionedAddressBook` will be initialized with the initial address book state, and the `currentStatePointer` pointing to that single address book state.

Step 2. The user executes `delete 5` command to delete the 5th person in the address book. The `delete` command calls `Model#commitAddressBook()`, causing the modified state of the address book after the `delete 5` command executes to be saved in the `addressBookStateList`, and the `currentStatePointer` is shifted to the newly inserted address book state.

Step 3. The user executes `add n/David …​` to add a new person. The `add` command also calls `Model#commitAddressBook()`, causing another modified address book state to be saved into the `addressBookStateList`.

<div markdown="span" class="alert alert-info">:information_source: **Note:** If a command fails its execution, it will not call `Model#commitAddressBook()`, so the address book state will not be saved into the `addressBookStateList`.

Step 4. The user now decides that adding the person was a mistake, and decides to undo that action by executing the `undo` command. The `undo` command will call `Model#undoAddressBook()`, which will shift the `currentStatePointer` once to the left, pointing it to the previous address book state, and restores the address book to that state.

<div markdown="span" class="alert alert-info">:information_source: **Note:** If the `currentStatePointer` is at index 0, pointing to the initial AddressBook state, then there are no previous AddressBook states to restore. The `undo` command uses `Model#canUndoAddressBook()` to check if this is the case. If so, it will return an error to the user rather
than attempting to perform the undo.

Similarly, how an undo operation goes through the `Model` component is shown below:

The `redo` command does the opposite — it calls `Model#redoAddressBook()`, which shifts the `currentStatePointer` once to the right, pointing to the previously undone state, and restores the address book to that state.

<div markdown="span" class="alert alert-info">:information_source: **Note:** If the `currentStatePointer` is at index `addressBookStateList.size() - 1`, pointing to the latest address book state, then there are no undone AddressBook states to restore. The `redo` command uses `Model#canRedoAddressBook()` to check if this is the case. If so, it will return an error to the user rather than attempting to perform the redo.

Step 5. The user then decides to execute the command `list`. Commands that do not modify the address book, such as `list`, will usually not call `Model#commitAddressBook()`, `Model#undoAddressBook()` or `Model#redoAddressBook()`. Thus, the `addressBookStateList` remains unchanged.

Step 6. The user executes `clear`, which calls `Model#commitAddressBook()`. Since the `currentStatePointer` is not pointing at the end of the `addressBookStateList`, all address book states after the `currentStatePointer` will be purged. Reason: It no longer makes sense to redo the `add n/David …​` command. This is the behavior that most modern desktop applications follow.

* **Auto-save**: Automatic saving of changes to persistent storage without requiring a separate save command.
* **CLI**: *Command-Line Interface*. An interface through which the user operates Cyclique primarily by typing text commands.

* **Cyclist**: A person whose contact and cycling-related information is stored and managed in Cyclique. The terms *rider* and *member* refer to the same concept; this documentation uses *cyclist* consistently.
* **Cyclist directory**: The collection of cyclist records stored in Cyclique.
* **Cycling organiser**: The primary user of Cyclique who manages cyclist records and organises recreational group rides.

* **Duplicate cyclist**: A cyclist entry with the same phone number or email address as an existing cyclist. Email comparison ignores letter case. Identical names alone do not make cyclists duplicates.
* **Experience level**: A categorical indication of a cyclist's riding experience. Cyclique uses three experience levels: **Beginner**, **Intermediate**, and **Advanced**.

* **Functional Threshold Power (FTP)**: A cyclist's cycling performance metric, measured in watts (W), representing the highest power they can approximately sustain for an extended period. In Cyclique, FTP is recorded as a whole number from 1 to 600 W.

* **Group ride**: An organised cycling session involving one or more cyclists. The term *ride meetup* refers to the same concept; this documentation uses *group ride* unless a feature specifically uses the term *ride meetup*.
* **GUI**: *Graphical User Interface*. The visual interface through which Cyclique displays cyclist information and command results.
* **JAR file**: A Java Archive file used to package and distribute the Cyclique application.
* **Java 25**: The minimum Java platform version required to run Cyclique, based on the project constraints.
* **Local storage**: Data stored on the user's own computer rather than on a remote server.
* **Mainstream OS**: Windows, Linux, Unix, or macOS
* **Parameter prefix**: A command prefix that identifies the type of value being supplied, such as `n/` for name, `p/` for phone number, `sos/` for emergency contact number, or `f/` for FTP.
* **Persistent data**: Data that remains available after Cyclique is closed and reopened.

* **Preferred cycling location**: A location where a cyclist prefers to ride or participate in group rides. A cyclist may have more than one preferred cycling location. The special value `any`, supplied as `l/any`, indicates that the cyclist has no location restriction and is considered to match every ride location.
* **Private contact detail**: A contact detail that is not meant to be shared with others
* **Ride roster**: The list of cyclists registered or confirmed to participate in a particular group ride.
* **Validation**: The process of checking whether user input satisfies Cyclique's specified input rules before accepting it.

AddressBook Level 3 (AB3) is a **desktop application for managing contacts, optimized for use through a Command Line Interface (CLI)** while retaining the benefits of a Graphical User Interface (GUI). If you type quickly, AB3 can help you manage contacts faster than traditional GUI applications.
1. Ensure that Java `25` or later is installed on your computer.
**Mac users:** Ensure you have the precise JDK version prescribed [here](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/javaInstallationMac.html).

1. Open a terminal, `cd` to the folder containing the JAR file, and run `java -jar cyclique.jar`.
A GUI similar to the one below should appear in a few seconds. Note how the app contains some sample data.
1. Type a command in the command box and press Enter to execute it. For example, type **`help`** and press Enter to open the help window.
Some example commands you can try:
* `add n/John Doe p/+65 98765432 sos/+65 99999999 e/johnd@example.com f/300 x/Beginner l/any` : Adds a contact named `John Doe` to the Address Book.
* `delete +65 98765432` : Requests deletion of the contact with this phone number. Enter `yes` to confirm or `no` to cancel.

Cyclists are displayed alphabetically by their full name, ignoring letter case, on startup
and after `list` or `find`. Adding a cyclist places them in the correct alphabetical position;
editing their name updates their position. Names that are identical ignoring case retain
their relative stored order. The visible indexes run consecutively from 1 within the current
display, including filtered results. Use phone numbers to target `edit` and `delete` as usual.
* Words in `UPPER_CASE` are the parameters to be supplied by the user.
For example, in `add n/NAME`, replace `NAME` with a value such as `John Doe`.
* Items in square brackets are optional.
For example, `edit PHONE [n/NAME] [f/FTP]` can be used as `edit +65 91234567 n/John Doe` or `edit +65 91234567 f/300`.
* Items followed by `…`​ can appear zero or more times.
For example, `[l/LOCATION]…` in `edit` may be omitted, or written as `l/Punggol` or `l/Punggol l/Marina Bay`.
* Parameters can be in any order.
For example, if the command specifies `n/NAME p/PHONE_NUMBER`, `p/PHONE_NUMBER n/NAME` is also acceptable.
* Extraneous parameters for commands that take no parameters, such as `help`, `list`, `exit`, and `clear`, are ignored.

### Locating persons by name, phone or emergency number: `find`
Finds persons by name keywords, phone numbers and emergency contact numbers.
Format: `find [n/NAME_KEYWORD]… [p/PHONE]… [sos/EMERGENCY_PHONE]…` (at least one field is required)
* Each `n/` takes one name keyword. Name matching is case-insensitive and requires a full word; for example, `n/hans` matches `Hans` but `n/Han` does not.
* Each `p/` takes one complete phone number. Phone matching is exact; `p/+65 963` does not match `+65 96320842`.
* Multiple values for the same field use `OR`: `find n/Hans n/Bo` returns people named `Hans Gruber` or `Bo Yang`.
* Each `sos/` takes one complete emergency contact number and uses the same phone validation and exact matching as `p/`. Repeated `sos/` values match any of those numbers.
* When multiple fields are supplied, a person must match every supplied field. Prefix order does not matter.
* Name keywords, phone numbers and emergency contact numbers search only their respective fields.
* `find sos/+65 99999999` lists cyclists with that emergency number.
* `find n/alex p/+65 96320842` returns only people whose name contains `alex` and whose phone number is `+65 96320842`.

Adds a group ride that an organiser plans to lead.
Format: `rideadd n/NAME from/FROM to/TO l/LOCATION d/DISTANCE f/MINIMUM_POWER s/MAX_GROUP_SIZE [notes/NOTES]`
`n/NAME` | The name of the ride. Letters, numbers and spaces only; it must not be blank.
`from/FROM` | When the ride starts, written as `DD-MM-YYYY TTTT`. `TTTT` is the time on a 24-hour clock from `0000` to `2359`, for example `18-10-2026 0630`. The date must be a real date.
`to/TO` | When the ride ends, in the same format as `from/`. It must not be earlier than `from/` (the same time is allowed).
`l/LOCATION` | One location. Letters, numbers, spaces, hyphens and apostrophes only.
`d/DISTANCE` | The distance in kilometres. A positive number with at most 2 decimal places, such as `45` or `45.5`.
`f/MINIMUM_POWER` | The minimum power a cyclist needs to join, in watts. A whole number from 1 to 600, the same range as a cyclist's FTP.
`s/MAX_GROUP_SIZE` | The most cyclists that can join. A positive whole number.
Every field except `notes/` is required, and each prefix can be used only once. You can give the fields in any order.

Each new ride gets an ID automatically: 1 for the first ride, 2 for the next and so on. IDs follow the order in which rides are created, are never reused, and carry on from where they stopped after you restart the app. A new ride has no cyclists on its roster yet. Two rides may have the same name, because rides are told apart by their IDs.

The ride is shown in the result box when it is added, and it is saved with your other data. The window also has a **Rides** panel in a column on the right (about 30% of the window width), next to the command box, result box and cyclist list. Each ride is shown as a card, like the cyclist cards. The card shows the ride's ID and name in a yellow-tinted heading, then its start and end, then labelled lines for the location, distance, minimum power and maximum group size, and a **Notes** line if the ride has notes. Long names, locations and notes wrap onto more lines, so the panel never needs a horizontal scrollbar. Click a ride to highlight its card. If there are no rides, the panel says `No rides yet. Use rideadd to create one.`

AddressBook data is saved automatically as a JSON file `[JAR file location]/data/addressbook.json`. Older data files may contain `address` or `tags` fields; Cyclique ignores them and omits them when saving, while retaining all supported cyclist details. Group rides are saved in the same file under `rides`, together with a `nextRideId` number that stops ride IDs from being reused; data files saved before rides existed still load, with no rides. Advanced users are welcome to update data directly by editing that data file.

If your changes make the data file invalid, AddressBook starts with an empty address book at the next run. The invalid file remains on disk until you run a command (AddressBook saves after every command). Still, we recommend backing up the file before editing it.

Furthermore, certain edits can cause the AddressBook to behave in unexpected ways (e.g., if a value entered is outside of the acceptable range). Therefore, edit the data file only if you are confident that you can update it correctly.
**Q**: How do I transfer my data to another computer?

Cyclique adapts AddressBook Level 3 (AB3) for organisers of recreational cycling
groups in Singapore. This MVP supports adding, finding, editing and deleting cyclists
with cycling profiles. The following changes are new compared with AB3.
* **Cycling profiles:** Cyclist records now include Functional Threshold Power (FTP)
in watts, experience level and preferred cycling locations alongside name, phone,
email and tags. Adding a cyclist requires FTP, experience level and at least one
preferred location. FTP accepts whole numbers from 1 to 600 W; experience levels
are Beginner, Intermediate or Advanced, ignoring case. Organisers can supply
multiple `l/LOCATION` fields or use `l/any` alone for no preference.
Blank or invalid locations are rejected,
duplicate locations are ignored regardless of case, and `any` cannot be mixed
* **Cycling fields throughout the workflow:** FTP and locations are included in
add, edit and delete confirmations and in the cards shown by `list` and `find`.
They are saved to JSON and loaded again on restart. Sample cyclists and command
examples use phone numbers in the required international-style format and
* **Complete cyclist cards:** A compact layout separates contact details from the
cycling profile. Cards display all seven fields, show FTP with the `W` unit and
display `l/any` as `Any`. Locations and tags appear in a consistent order in the
* **Alphabetical lists:** Cyclists are displayed alphabetically by full name,
ignoring letter case. The order updates after additions, name edits and searches,
making cyclists easier to locate without changing their saved order. Names that
compare equally retain their relative order, and displayed indexes remain consecutive.
* **Phone-based editing and deletion:** `edit` and `delete` identify cyclists by
their phone number instead of AB3's list index. Both commands act on the displayed
list, and ambiguous matches are rejected. This keeps targeting consistent when
the list is sorted or filtered. A cyclist hidden by a filter cannot be edited or
deleted until displayed, preventing commands from acting on an unseen record.
* **Editable cycling details:** Organisers can update FTP, experience level and
preferred locations using `edit`, alongside existing contact fields and tags.
Omitted fields retain their values; supplied locations replace the previous set.
* **Name and phone searches:** `find` now requires prefixed criteria: each `n/`
supplies one complete name word, and each `p/` supplies one exact phone number.
Repeat the prefix for multiple values, such as `find n/Alex n/Bernice`. Values
within a field use OR (either value can match); combining name and phone criteria
uses AND (both fields must match). Name matching ignores case.
* **Stronger duplicate checks:** `add` and `edit` reject cyclists who share a phone
number or email with another record, including records hidden by a filter. Email
comparison ignores case. Cyclists with the same name remain allowed when their
phone numbers and emails are unique. An edit can retain the cyclist's own unique
phone number, and rejected duplicate operations leave existing records unchanged.
* **International phone format:** Phone numbers must contain `+`, one to three
country-code digits, exactly one separating space and at least three number
digits, for example `+65 91234567`. Hyphens and parentheses are rejected with
* **Updated appearance and command help:** Cyclique has a dark theme with yellow
accents, rounded cyclist cards and cycling artwork on startup and exit. A taller
command input makes commands easier to read and edit. The Help dropdown shows all
eight commands and inserts starter text into the command box. Its edit format now
The full Help window lists command formats and examples and opens through
* **Residential addresses removed:** Cyclique focuses on preferred cycling
locations rather than residential addresses. The `a/` field has been removed from
commands, cyclist records and saved output. Older files containing an `address`
field can still be loaded: it is ignored and omitted on the next save. These files
must still contain valid names, emails and experience levels, phone numbers in the
current format, and unique phone numbers and emails. Missing FTP defaults to 1 W,
and missing or empty locations default to `any`; supplied FTP and location values
must pass validation. Unmodified AB3 data files are not directly compatible.
